Ancient of Days (Doctrinal)
AYN-shunt of days
noun
Aramaic Attiq Yomin (Dan 7:9, 13, 22) — "Ancient of Days"; God enthroned in eternal judgment in Daniel's vision, before whom the Son of Man is presented and given an everlasting kingdom.

Biblical Definition

Ancient of Days is the title Daniel gave to God in his vision of the heavenly courtroom (Dan 7:9-14, 22), the only place in Scripture where this exact title appears. The vision: "I beheld till the thrones were cast down, and the Ancient of days did sit, whose garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like the pure wool: his throne was like the fiery flame, and his wheels as burning fire" (Dan 7:9). The four beasts of empires past pass before Him; the books are opened; the dominion is taken away from the beast and given to one "like the Son of man" who is brought near before the Ancient of Days (Dan 7:13-14). The Son of Man receives "dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed." This is the throne-room scene Christ explicitly references at His own trial (Matt 26:64 — "hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven"). The Ancient of Days is the Father giving the kingdom to the Son; the white hair is the OT picture of God's eternity and judgment; the fiery throne is the seat from which empires are weighed and Christ is crowned. Revelation 1:14 applies the white-as-snow-hair imagery directly to the risen Christ — the Ancient of Days and the Son of Man are co-glorified, two persons of the Triune God seated together over history.

Webster 1828 Definition

God enthroned as eternal Judge in Daniel's vision; presents the Son of Man with an everlasting kingdom; the white-hair imagery applied to the risen Christ in Rev 1:14.

ANCIENT OF DAYS, noun. The title of God in Daniel's vision of the heavenly courtroom (Dan 7:9-14, 22). Aramaic Attiq Yomin.

Enthroned, white-haired, with fiery throne. Receives the Son of Man and gives Him everlasting dominion. Imagery applied to the risen Christ in Rev 1:14.

Key Scripture

Daniel 7:9 — "I beheld till the thrones were cast down, and the Ancient of days did sit, whose garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like the pure wool: his throne was like the fiery flame, and his wheels as burning fire."

Daniel 7:13-14 — "I saw in the night visions, and, behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days... And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom."

Matthew 26:64 — "Jesus saith unto him, Thou hast said: nevertheless I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven."

Revelation 1:14 — "His head and his hairs were white like wool, as white as snow; and his eyes were as a flame of fire."

Modern Corruption

Ancient of Days is corrupted when modalist or unitarian readings collapse the Father and Son into one Person (the canonical vision shows them as distinct), or when the Daniel 7 throne-room scene is treated as mere apocalyptic poetry rather than as the prophetic source Christ Himself ratified.

expand to see more

Modalist collapse. The Daniel 7 vision shows the Ancient of Days enthroned AND the Son of Man brought to Him to receive dominion — TWO distinct persons in the heavenly court. Modalist readings (one God appearing in three modes) or unitarian readings (Jesus as exalted creature, not coequal with the Father) cannot accommodate this. Christ's explicit self-application of Dan 7:13 at His trial (Matt 26:64) confirms: He claimed to be the Son of Man who would receive dominion from the Ancient of Days. The Trinity is implicit in Daniel 7 before it is explicit in the NT.

Apocalyptic-poetry dismissal. Some modernist commentary treats Daniel 7 as late-second-century BC pseudonymous apocalyptic — a literary form to be appreciated but not received as predictive. But Christ Himself quoted it in His most solemn moment (His trial before the Sanhedrin) and on the most weighty subject (His own divine identity and return). To strip Daniel 7 of its prophetic weight is to deny what Christ Himself ratified.
